title: Dirichlet's theorem generalizes to arithmetic progressions: if $\gcd(a,d) = 1...

problemStatement.plain: Formal investigation in number theory: Dirichlet's theorem generalizes to arithmetic progressions: if $\gcd(a,d) = 1....

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETED: Full proof of infinitely many primes ≡ 2 (mod 3). 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
builtItems: theorem infinitely_many_primes_2_mod_3: ∀ n, ∃ p prime, p > n ∧ p % 3 = 2
theorem primes_2_mod_3_infinite: Set.Infinite {p | Prime p ∧ p % 3 = 2}
lemma mul_mod_three_one: product of 1-mod-3 integers stays 1-mod-3
lemma prime_mod_three: primes ≠ 3 are 1 or 2 mod 3
lemma factors_determine_mod_three: n with all prime factors = 3 or ≡ 1 mod 3 cannot be ≡ 2 mod 3
lemma has_prime_factor_2_mod_3: n ≡ 2 mod 3 implies prime factor ≡ 2 mod 3
insights: Proof mirrors 4k+3 argument exactly: use N = 3·(n+1)!-1 ≡ 2 (mod 3)
Key: product of 1-mod-3 factors gives 1-mod-3, so N must have a 2-mod-3 factor
Strong induction on n used in factors_determine_mod_three (same as 4k+3 version)
The general Dirichlet theorem requires L-functions, but residue -1 mod d always has elementary proof
Pattern generalizes: infinitely many primes ≡ d-1 (mod d) for any d ≥ 2
nextSteps: Potential: prove primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) requires quadratic reciprocity (harder case)
Potential: unify all -1-mod-d proofs into a single parametric theorem
